lab_title: VSEPR in AR: From Lewis Structures to 3D Molecular Geometry
top_level_objectives: Connect Lewis structures to VSEPR electron-domain counts (bonding pairs vs lone pairs)
Use the five electron-domain geometries to predict molecular geometry for common molecules
Explain and quantify how lone pairs change bond angles and molecular shape (including characteristic deviations)
Validate VSEPR predictions by comparing AR-modeled geometries to real-world examples (H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, XeF4)

scenes.brief_purpose: Translate a drawn Lewis structure into electron domains around a central atom, distinguishing bonding pairs from lone pairs.
key_visuals: A centered Lewis structure hologram with the central atom highlighted
Callouts that mark bonding pairs and lone pairs as distinct “domain” icons radiating from the central atom
A small checklist UI: total domains, lone pairs count, bonding pairs count
student_actions: Select/confirm which electron pairs in the Lewis structure are lone pairs vs bonding pairs
Count the electron domains around the central atom and report the total number and lone-pair count in the prompt
Predict the starting electron-domain geometry category (linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral) based on the domain count

scenes.scene_name: Scene 2 — Building the Base Electron-Domain Geometry
scenes.brief_purpose: Establish the idealized shapes for each electron-domain geometry and the idea of minimizing repulsion.
key_visuals: A ghosted ideal geometry (e.g., tetrahedral, trigonal planar, etc.) appearing around the central atom
Colored arrows/lines showing repulsion vectors between electron domains
Angle labels for ideal values (180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°/120°, 180°) matching the selected domain type
student_actions: Choose the AR “arrange domains” mode and position the electron-domain markers so they settle into the ideal geometry
Observe the repulsion-guided motion and pause when the system indicates it reached a minimum-repulsion configuration
State the ideal electron-domain geometry and its ideal bond angles for later comparison

scenes.scene_name: Scene 3 — Lone-Pair Effects Within Each Electron Geometry
scenes.brief_purpose: Show how lone pairs alter the molecular geometry by occupying more space and pushing bonding pairs into new positions.
key_visuals: A side-by-side comparison: electron-domain model vs molecular-shape model for the same domain arrangement
A visual “angular space” heatmap emphasizing lone-pair regions as larger repulsion zones
Examples of lone-pair-modified outcomes emerging as labels (bent, trigonal pyramidal, trigonal bipyramidal derivatives, square planar, square pyramidal)
student_actions: Reassign one or more domains as lone pairs in the AR interface and watch bonding domains reposition
Match the resulting molecular geometry label to the scenario (e.g., bent vs linear; trigonal pyramidal vs tetrahedral)
Record how bond angles shift relative to the idealized geometry and identify the direction of deviation (smaller when lone pairs are present)

scenes.scene_name: Scene 4 — Case Study: Water, Ammonia, Methane
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply VSEPR predictions to molecules with well-known bond angles and connect to experimentally observed deviations.
key_visuals: AR models for H2O, NH3, and CH4 appearing as selectable cards
Water: labeled 104.5° bond angle; Methane: 109.5° reference; Ammonia: intermediate trigonal-pyramidal angle
A “lone pair vs bond pair” angular-space overlay for each molecule
student_actions: For each molecule, count electron domains and determine the molecular geometry predicted by VSEPR
Drag angle probes to measure (or read) the AR bond angle and compare to the labeled real/typical values
Explain, using VSEPR reasoning, why the bond angle in H2O is smaller than in CH4

scenes.scene_name: Scene 5 — Trigonal Bipyramidal and Octahedral Derivatives
scenes.brief_purpose: Predict and differentiate complex molecular shapes arising from trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron domains with lone pairs.
key_visuals: Selectable molecule set: PF5 (no lone pairs), SF6 (two?) and XeF4 (two?) shown as AR holograms
A trigonal bipyramidal framework with distinct axial vs equatorial positions clearly highlighted
An octahedral framework with axial/equatorial sites, and labels for square planar, seesaw, T-shaped, and square pyramidal outcomes
student_actions: Choose one molecule at a time and identify electron-domain type (trigonal bipyramidal vs octahedral)
Place lone pairs in the appropriate positions (e.g., influence axial/equatorial preference) and finalize the minimum-repulsion arrangement
State the predicted molecular geometry (e.g., seesaw/T-shaped for XeF4’s related domain case; square planar vs square pyramidal) and justify which lone pairs occupy which sites

scenes.scene_name: Scene 6 — Compare Predictions to Real Structures (Wrap-Up Check)
scenes.brief_purpose: Synthesize the lab by validating predicted geometries against observed structures and consolidating the VSEPR workflow.
key_visuals: A summary dashboard: Lewis → electron domains → electron-domain geometry → molecular geometry → predicted bond angles
A “match” interface where predicted vs observed structure icons can be aligned for each molecule (H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, XeF4)
Common-shape gallery with geometry names and key distinguishing features (lone pairs count and angle deviation cues)
student_actions: For each target molecule, confirm the full prediction chain and correct any mismatches
Briefly compare trends: increasing lone pairs decreases ideal bond angles and changes shape (name the trend)
Submit a final explanation: how minimizing repulsion and accounting for lone-pair space leads to the observed geometries
